content: 1. The management of extensive carious lesions often involves excavation and restoration, or in severe cases, extraction of the affected teeth. 2. A caries management pathway, guided by diagnostic information, can assist clinicians in determining whether to pursue preventive measures or develop a treatment plan. 3. One recently developed caries management system is the International Caries Classification and Management System (ICCMS), introduced by Ismail in 2015. 4. The ICCMS outlines three management approaches: For sound dentition, clinicians implement preventive strategies to maintain the integrity of tooth surfaces and prevent caries development. For early lesions, non-invasive treatments are employed to halt the decay process, promote remineralization, and prevent progression to cavitated decay. For advanced caries, management involves excavation and restoration or, in some cases, extraction. 5. The ability to accurately detect early caries and optimize preventive strategies is central to this care pathway. 6. Detecting and diagnosing early caries remains challenging, with a high likelihood of undiagnosed early disease, as noted by Ekstrand in 1997. 7. When early lesions are missed, opportunities to prevent progression to cavitated decay or reverse the disease process are lost, leading to the need for restorative interventions, as highlighted by Ekstrand in 1998. 8. Dental clinicians have access to a variety of treatment options, depending on the severity of the observed disease. 9. Initial caries can often be managed non-surgically through preventive and remineralizing approaches, such as plaque control, dietary counseling, and fluoride application, as described by Kidd in 2016. 10. Minimally invasive treatments for early caries include sealing the affected tooth surface or infiltrating demineralized tissue with resins. 11. High-risk patients with severe caries may require stepwise caries removal and restoration of extensive lesions. 12. Visual and tactile dental examinations are the cornerstone of caries detection, with research on their accuracy dating back over half a century (Backer Dirks, 1951). 13. A range of diagnostic tests is available to support different stages of the care pathway, particularly for detecting and diagnosing disease (Bloemendal, 2004; Fyffe, 2000). 14. Visual or visual-tactile examinations involve identifying caries based on their appearance, aided by a dental mirror and probe, on clean and dry teeth. While fundamental, this method has limitations in diagnosing early lesions. 15. Radiography, particularly bitewing radiology, is a commonly used adjunct to visual examinations, aiding in the detection of caries and providing information on lesion depth and severity (Wenzel, 1995; Whaites, 2013). 16. Advanced radiographic techniques, such as subtraction radiographs and cone beam computed tomography (CBCT), offer enhanced diagnostic capabilities but come with increased radiation exposure (Horner, 2009). 17. Digital radiographic methods provide benefits such as rapid image viewing and the ability to manipulate images for improved clarity (Wenzel, 2006). 18. Fluorescence-based methods detect changes in enamel structure caused by caries. Diseased teeth respond differently to light-induced fluorescence compared to sound teeth, allowing for potential quantification of mineral loss (Angmar-Månsson, 2001; Matos, 2011). 19. Fluorescence techniques, such as laser fluorescence and light fluorescence, can help identify early caries that may not be visible during a standard visual examination. 20. Quantitative light-induced fluorescence (QLF) emits green or red light and can determine whether a lesion is active or arrested. 21. Fibre-optic transillumination (FOTI) uses light emitted from a handheld device to illuminate the tooth, aiding in the detection of caries (Pretty, 2006). 22. Each diagnostic method has its advantages and disadvantages. For example, visual examinations are quick and cost-effective but may miss early lesions or fail to assess lesion depth. Radiographs are more sensitive for detecting proximal and occlusal lesions but involve radiation exposure. Fluorescence methods can detect subtle changes in tooth structure but may have reliability concerns. 23. The choice of diagnostic method should be tailored to the patient’s needs, caries risk, and clinical context, balancing benefits and limitations.
